---
layout: post
title: "Let AI agents use your SSH keys without handing them the keys"
description: I want agents to pull, push a working branch and open PRs smoothly. That requires separating credential use from credential theft and controlling what a credential can do.
category: Kai field notes
author: Sameeh Jubran
date: 2026-11-12 20:12:00 +0200
---

I want an agent to pull the repository I gave it, push its working branch and open a PR without stopping me at every step. That is routine development work. I also want the same agent unable to print my private key or ship a private project to somebody else's repository. Early Kai experiments made those wishes look contradictory. They are not, but the distinction is more precise than “allow GitHub.”

In one development test, Kai's experimental Files wall treated a Git push like a request to read an SSH key. Git started `ssh`, the key file open was denied, and the push failed with “Operation not permitted.” A Kai card came after the failed operation; approving it could not restart the push. The [test note](https://github.com/sameehj/kai/blob/master/docs/audit/live-tests/item1-ssh-live.md) later recorded a narrower success: with a key already loaded in `ssh-agent`, `git ls-remote` worked and a push completed its SSH handshake with no Kai cards in that run. That was a development build on one Mac, not a promise for every setup or a feature in Preview 2.

The mechanics explain why this path can work. [`ssh-agent`](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-agent.1) holds private key identities and answers authentication requests over a local socket. You load a key with [`ssh-add`](https://man.openbsd.org/ssh-add.1); the SSH client can then ask the agent to authenticate without reading the private key file itself for that operation. On macOS, Apple's `ssh-add --apple-use-keychain` can store the key's **passphrase** in Keychain when adding the key to the agent. It does not mean Keychain has replaced repository permissions, and it does not give Kai a new policy boundary. [GitHub's macOS instructions](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent?platform=mac) describe that setup.

Opening a PR is another path. `gh pr create` talks to the GitHub API and normally authenticates with a token. The GitHub CLI [stores that token in the system credential store when available](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_login), with a file fallback; it can also use a token from the environment. Choosing SSH for Git operations does not turn `gh`'s API calls into SSH. An agent can have a working `git push` and still need `gh` authentication for the PR. Conversely, protecting `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` says nothing about whether an agent can print a GitHub API token with `gh auth token`.

I want to protect credential bytes because copying them can let someone reuse them elsewhere. But an agent that can reach `ssh-agent` can ask it to authenticate. The key can remain unread while its authority is misused. An account key may have access to several repositories; a deploy key can be scoped to one repository, depending on how it was installed. [GitHub's deploy-key documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/managing-deploy-keys) makes that scope explicit. Neither choice tells a local tool whether this particular push matches what I asked the agent to do.

Here is the line I want a guard to draw. `git fetch origin` for the repository already checked out is normal. Pushing `feature/price-update` to that repository and running `gh pr create` is normal if I asked for a PR. A command that prints `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, copies it into a patch or calls `gh auth token` is credential extraction, not part of publishing a branch. A force-push to `master`, `gh repo delete`, or a change to collaborators is a destructive or privileged operation. Those should need an explicit decision unless an adequate one has already been made.

The destination needs the same precision. `git remote add backup git@github.com:someone-else/private-copy.git` followed by a push might use the same SSH key and the same `github.com` hostname as `git@github.com:my-team/project.git`. The owner and repository are different. A network rule that approves `github.com:22` permits a connection to that host; it cannot by itself approve a particular repository or branch. Deciding whether a push belongs to the authorized workspace needs the remote URL, repository identity, command context and an enforcement point that actually observes them. Host-level approval alone does not provide that.

There are useful limits even to that more specific policy. A hook can inspect a supported Git command before the agent runs it, but a script can construct a command or use another library after the hook's view ends. A network filter may see a connection to GitHub while seeing neither the Git remote nor the payload. A “read secret, then connect” signal can call attention to a risky sequence; failing to observe the read is not evidence that an upload is harmless. I would rather state these gaps than call a hostname a complete exfiltration rule.

The current [Preview 2 release](https://github.com/sameehj/kai/releases/tag/v0.2.0-preview.2) has supported agent hooks and an Internet wall in Watch mode. It does not ship repository-aware Git rules or an operating-system Files wall. [PR #12](https://github.com/sameehj/kai/pull/12) addresses a different piece of the friction, routine MCP approvals and broken hooks; its passing tests do not validate Git authorization. The repository and credential checks described here are proposals in the redesign plan, still needing implementation and live replay for SSH and HTTPS, `gh`, destructive commands and new remotes.

The goal is a workday in which a branch push feels like a branch push, not like a secret theft attempt, while a request to export a credential or send code to a different owner receives a clear stop. The key can stay secret, and I still need to decide what authority I am letting the agent exercise.
